Spotting the Difference: Genuine Gospel Ministry vs. Spiritual Fraud

Paul answers the charge that he is just another charlatan — and in doing so shows how to determine the difference between fake and genuine gospel ministry: its motivation, its outworking, and its fruit.

Josh Lean
39 min
Captured live
with Ahtend

Real or Fake?

How do you determine the difference between fake and genuine gospel ministry? You and I now live in a world of fake news and deception. We have learned to be suspicious, and often we are right to be. Frauds do exist, and they are wolves in sheep's clothing.

Wolfgang Beltracchi is regarded as the most successful art forger in history. For decades his work hung in serious collections, and nobody could tell. What finally exposed him was not an expert's eye but a laboratory: a pigment in the paint that had not been manufactured when the original was supposedly created.

WORK
Rotes Bild mit Pferden

Sold as a lost German expressionist canvas of 1914. In 2008 an owner had it forensically tested and the paint turned out not to have existed in 1914 — one test, and thirty years of forgeries came apart.

PERSON
Wolfgang Beltracchi

A 75-year-old German, and the most successful art forger of all time. He forged over 300 works; just 14 of them were valued at over $45 million.

That is the uncomfortable question this passage puts to us. The fake looked right until someone tested it. So how do you spot the difference?

Point 1

Motivation of Gospel Ministry

How do you tell a real work from a fake one? Paul separates himself from the itinerant philosophers of his day, who won crowds by flattery and worked for profit. His visit produced fruit — it was "not without results".

"We speak as those approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel. We are not trying to please people but God, who tests our hearts. You know we never used flattery, nor did we put on a mask to cover up greed."

1 Thessalonians 2:4–5

Paul begins by pointing back to what happened when he came to Thessalonica. His visit, he says, was not without results — quite literally, that word means "not in vain, not empty". Unlike the philosophers in the area, who were blurring and blowing out their substance, there was substance to the ministry he brought.

INSIGHT
Character is tied to results

Paul had been "treated outrageously" at Philippi — beaten and imprisoned (Acts 16) — and still pressed on. There was no financial upside. The mistreatment is the proof, not the exception.

There was no financial upside to any of this. He was not working from flattery, or greed, or a desire for praise from people.

One of my favourite films is Cool Runnings. In the middle of it the American coach tries to discourage the Jamaicans from starting their bobsled team. He calls them together, shows them videos of sleds crashing everywhere, and tells them that their bones will not break in a bobsled — they shatter. Then the lights come up and he asks: so who wants in? The room clears out except for three men.

"There is one minor drawback to this delightful winter sport, and that is the high-speed crashes. Always remember — your bones will not break in a bobsled. No, no. They shatter."

Cool Runnings (1993) — John Candy as coach Irv Blitzer

He was not recruiting people who wanted to build a reputation and a personal following. Neither was Paul.

Point 2

The Outworking of Gospel Ministry

Not performative — relational. Paul moves from why he ministers to how.

INSIGHT
Encourage, comfort, urge

"As a father deals with his own children." The same three verbs you would use with your own wife and children — pushing them to live lives worthy of the gospel.

He reaches for the most ordinary and most demanding image available: a nursing mother caring for her children.

"Just as a nursing mother cares for her children, so we cared for you. Because we loved you so much, we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God but our lives as well. … For you know that we dealt with each of you as a father deals with his own children, encouraging, comforting and urging you to live lives worthy of God."

1 Thessalonians 2:7–12
INSIGHT
"Not open for business until 9 a.m."

"What time do nursing mums have to get up to feed their children? Anytime. I've never heard of a nursing mother saying 'I'm not open for business until 9 a.m.' But I certainly watch my wife when babies cry — she wakes up at 2 o'clock in the morning."

In the first century it was not uncommon for a family to hire a nurse to feed, protect and educate an infant. Paul's point is that he did not do that. We didn't hire you out. We didn't pass you on to someone else. We loved you so much that we did it ourselves — gently, patiently and tenderly.

The heart of gospel ministry is not a talking head who preaches the word well but does not care for the lives of the people he shepherds. You can listen to almost anyone's sermon in the world now. But they do not live in your context. Don't confuse a quick wizard who can wield God's word with the godly shepherd.

"I am the good shepherd; I know my sheep and my sheep know me — just as the Father knows me and I know the Father — and I lay down my life for the sheep."

John 10:14–15
From the talk

Leaders are not trying to be Jesus. They are under-shepherds, pointing not to themselves but to him. "How good does it sound that Jesus knows you today? You can walk out of here and go: 'I'm not a nobody, I'm a somebody to Jesus. He knows my name.'"

IN SHORT
A quick wizard, or a godly shepherd

You can stream anyone's sermon on YouTube or a podcast — but "they do not live in your context."

INSIGHT
Seed and rain

Plant a seed, the rain falls, it sprouts. The word of God is what is at work — not the persuasiveness of the messenger. "The question is not whether you've got a big brain, but whether you love God."

Jesus is the good shepherd.

Point 3

The Fruit of Gospel Ministry

What grows when the word is received as what it actually is.

"And we also thank God continually because, when you received the word of God which you heard from us, you accepted it not as a human word, but as it actually is, the word of God, which is indeed at work in you who believe."

1 Thessalonians 2:13

Look what happens: you became imitators of God's churches in Judea. Just as the gospel was growing in those churches, so it was growing here — and so was the opposition. That the suffering continues is evidence the faith is real, not evidence against it.

INSIGHT
You became imitators

"For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of God's churches in Judea." They suffered the same things from their own people that the Judean churches suffered. Growth looked the same — and so did the opposition. Josh's interpretation: our instinct should not be to differentiate ourselves from other churches, but to find the commonalities in the word of God.

A very old pastor, before a church voted on whether to receive him, told them: I will do two things if you appoint me to this role. First, I will teach the Bible to you. And second, I will help you to die well.

"I'm not coming to please you. My job is not to make church comfortable for you… I'll help you to trust in the Lord even on the day you die."

A very old pastor, before the church voted to receive him

So: do you want pastors who please people, or who please God?

The Challenge

INSIGHT
Close enough to carry the scent

If a pastor doesn't smell like the sheep, he shouldn't be a shepherd of God's people. The shepherd is not above the flock or adjacent to it — he is close enough to carry its scent, to carry the mess and the mark of the lives of those he serves.

We began by asking what genuine gospel ministry actually is. Paul's answer is clear enough to hold on to. It is motivated by a desire to please God rather than people. It is worked out through the sharing of our lives, so that we encourage one another to keep pursuing Jesus in the middle of the mess and the muck. And it bears gospel fruit.

INSIGHT
The line, stated plainly

"If a pastor doesn't want to get involved in the mess and the muck of the lives of those they serve, they should not be a shepherd of God's people." Balanced by: "don't have superhuman expectations of your pastors and elders. They can't be at everything and do everything for you."

So there is a challenge here for all of us. Pray that pastors and elders would want to please God more than they want to please you. And then pray that we would not settle for being a happy little place to come and enjoy ourselves — that we would long to please him, and love one another enough to share our lives even in the mess. That is a frightening thing to pray for.

QUESTION
Is a pastor an employee of the family or part of the family?

The New Testament's dominant metaphor for the local church is the family of God. Paul's answer: not administrative distance above you, but "alongside you and involved in the mess of your lives".

The prayer he left them with was small and specific: Lord, help me to get in among at least one other person in the mess and the muck that is going on in their life, and to love them even in the midst of that.

One of my greatest joys as a pastor is watching people go through genuinely terrible seasons and keep loving God through them — even in the face of death. Proving over and over again:

Jesus is good. Jesus is worthy. And there is a day coming when he is going to make all things right.

That is the kind of faith God wants to grow in each of us: to keep loving him in light of the eternity which is coming.

In closing

For whose praise?

"Father, we really do cry that you would help us to be the kind of church that lives not for the praise of man, but earnestly for your praise and your glory and your honour."
